after: ## Charge, current and energy: the picture
alt: A 6.0 V battery and a lamp in a loop. Conventional current runs from + to −, electrons drift the other way. Each coulomb gains 6.0 J in the battery and transfers it in the lamp. Side notes: Q = I × t, voltage is energy per unit charge, E = Q × V.
caption: Charge is not used up: each coulomb picks up energy at the supply and transfers it in the components.

after: ## Charge, current and energy: the picture
alt: Left: 0.80 A enters a junction and splits into 0.30 A and 0.50 A. Middle: in series the supply voltage is shared, V supply = V₁ + V₂. Right: in parallel each branch has the full supply voltage.
caption: Current in equals current out at a junction; series shares the voltage, parallel branches each get all of it.

alt: Left: three lamps in series with one broken; all go out. Right: three lamps in parallel, each with its own switch; one lamp is broken but the other two stay lit.
caption: In parallel each lamp gets the full voltage, has its own switch and keeps working if another fails.

alt: A 9.0 V battery with 120 Ω and 60 Ω resistors in series. Total 180 Ω gives 0.050 A, so the resistors have 6.0 V and 3.0 V across them. In 2.0 minutes 6.0 C flows and the battery transfers 54 J.
caption: Total resistance first, then current, then each voltage; check they add to the supply.

alt: Circuit with a supply, an ammeter and a variable resistor in series with the component under test, and a voltmeter connected across the component. Steps: take at least six readings, reverse the component, and plot current against voltage.
caption: Vary the resistor, read V and I, reverse the component, and plot I against V.

after: ## I−V characteristics and how to investigate them (2.9)
alt: Current against voltage for three components. A wire or resistor gives a straight line through the origin. A filament lamp gives a curve that flattens in both directions. A diode passes almost no current in reverse and a steeply rising current once a small forward voltage is exceeded.
caption: Straight line: constant resistance. Flattening curve: resistance rising. Diode: one direction only.

alt: An LDR and, separately, a thermistor each in series with a fixed resistor, an ammeter and a battery. More light or a higher temperature lowers the sensor resistance, so the current and the voltage across the fixed resistor rise while the voltage across the sensor falls.
caption: More light or more warmth: lower sensor resistance, larger current.

alt: A filament lamp I–V curve with two marked points: 2.0 V at 0.20 A gives 10 Ω, and 6.0 V at 0.30 A gives 20 Ω.
caption: On a curve, find R = V ÷ I at each point: here 10 Ω rises to 20 Ω.
